newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin brings in reformers to shake up government.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin brings in reformers to shake up government.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin set Russia on course for a new spell of profound economic and social change on Monday by naming a handful of liberal reformers in his most dramatic government reshuffle in five years.

In a suprise move analysts saw as an attempt to end feuding between his conservative and radical supporters, Yeltsin named 37-year-old Boris Nemtsov, a regional reform governor, as one of two first deputies to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, 58.

"Two young men -- you and Anatoly Chubais -- create a fresh young team in the government -- from scratch," Yeltsin told Nemtsov. The younger man later said the job would mean taking unpopular decisions that would wreck his political career.

Nemtsov, a media celebrity who Yeltsin says is presidential material, will spearhead welfare reforms and fight monopolies with the same rank as Yeltsin's former chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais, who will also have the title Finance Minister.

Last week, Yeltsin said Chubais, 41, would be the only first deputy. He may have changed his mind to mediate between the former privatisation chief and Chermomyrdin, former head of the state gas monopoly and seen as a defender of big business.
Chernomyrdin later announced his full eight-man complement of deputy premiers, down from 12. Including Chubais and Nemtsov, it revealed a clear tilt in the balance toward reformers.

"The hardships Russia is living through in social terms are connected to the work of the cabinet and all the changes in the government are aimed at correcting the course of reforms," Chernomyrdin told Russian journalists.

The prime minister, now in his fifth year in charge, said the changes answered Yeltsin's criticisms of the government in a hard-hitting state of the nation address on March 6. In it, the 66-year-old president declared his return from long illness and demanded urgent action to end the present economic crisis.
Trade unions, backed by the communist opposition-dominated parliament, plan a day of strikes and protests on March 27.
Many workers and pensioners have not been paid, creating what the opposition says is an explosive situation.
Yeltsin himself gave voice to the discontent of millions, saying on March 6: "People's patience is running out."

The president, re-elected last July against the odds after a campaign masterminded by Chubais, has seen his previous free market reforms get bound up in a web of graft and stagnation, notably among Soviet-era industrial monopolies.

The task for Chubais and Nemtsov, after the biggest cabinet shake-up since liberal Yegor Gaidar became post-Soviet Russia's first premier in 1991, will be to implement change in the face of inertia and deepening social discontent in the provinces.
The appointment of Nemtsov, from Nizhy Novgorod region, and of mayor of the industrial city of Samara, Oleg Sysuyev, as deputy premiers gives a more provincial look to the cabinet.
In a new attempt to kill off Soviet-style economic control, Chernomyrdin said some minstries, including the Industry Ministry, would be downgraded and brought into Chubais's domain.

Backing up Chubais, liberal Deputy Economy Minister Yakov Urinson steps up to become Deputy Prime Minister and Economy Minister. Alfred Kokh, effectively Russia's privatisation minister, was also promoted to Deputy Prime Minister.

A number of conservative ministers lost their jobs or were demoted, although Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov stays on as deputy prime minister. The fate of the other, lower-ranking "power ministers" was not clear. But Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov seems certain to stay on as does Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, despite a run-in with Yeltsin over army funding.
Other cabinet changes are due later this week.
Yeltsin's decisive moves also served as a reminder he is still in charge to the other players, including Chernomyrdin, who may be being groomed for the succession in the year 2000.

"I am in good form today. Today I am able, so to speak, to rule the state and in fact in better form today than before the illness and I will of course rule Russia up to new elections in 2000," Yeltsin said in an interview shown on Russian Television.

He reshuffled the government days before heading off to Helsinki for a summit with President Bill Clinton on Thursday and Friday. U.S. and Russian officials are seeking a deal to ease tensions over NATO's expansion plans.

Yeltsin made clear on Monday that Russia's patience was not endless. "I don't want a return to the Cold War, I don't want it and our people don't want it, but for that there must be equal conditions in the world order," he said.
